text:
maria: quick heads-up — running into truncated JSON from the SSE stream in the Swift SDK. last object sometimes ends mid-JSON, decoder throws and we drop the tail. seen on macOS + iOS simulator.

josh: yep saw similar yesterday on a client test. stream arrives as tiny frames under load, partial object boundaries.

anika: are you using a streaming incremental parser or just JSONSerialization on each chunk?

maria: we call JSONSerialization.jsonObject(with: chunk) per chunk right now, so it fails when chunk is incomplete.

ryan: that'll do it. you need to buffer leftover bytes and prepend to next chunk. also watch multibyte UTF-8 boundaries (emoji split).

maria: agreed. proposal: keep a "tail" buffer that we append incoming bytes to, then repeatedly try to parse a single top-level JSON value and slice off consumed bytes. if parse fails due to incomplete data, break and wait for next chunk.

sam: +1. we've got a tiny helper in go-client for this. i can paste pseudo-code.

ryan: paste would help.

sam: ```go
// naive reassembly loop
var tail []byte
for chunk := range stream {
  buf := append(tail, chunk...)
  for {
    obj, n, ok := tryParseJSON(buf) // returns bytes consumed
    if !ok { break }
    handle(obj)
    buf = buf[n:]
  }
  tail = buf // leftover for next iteration
}
```

leo: also make sure your parser returns an explicit needed-bytes vs error; many JSON libs only error which is ambiguous. tryParseJSON should detect EOF-like conditions vs malformed.

anika: for Python we use JSONDecoder.raw_decode which returns index. similar idea. for JS we feed bytes to a streaming parser (clarinet) that emits objects.

maria: two extra quirks we hit: 1) backpressure — when app-level consumer is slow we end up reading tiny fragments repeatedly (10-50 bytes) which exacerbates split objects. 2) auth refresh — occasional reconnects can leave tail orphaned.

josh: for backpressure we added a simple read-window: keep reading up to N bytes or until a newline/boundary heuristic, whichever first. buffersize 8k reduced splits. also applied micro-delay to consumer when queue length > threshold.

maria: good idea. i'm wary of heuristics though. prefer correct reassembly + stress tests.

ryan: agree. reassembly is correct. heuristics reduce CPU overhead and avoid pathological tiny reads. probably both: robust parser + optional read buffer increase.

anika: on auth reconnects, make sure to persist tail across reconnect attempts unless you explicitly discard stream state. and add a max-tail size guard in case of corrupt stream.

maria: i'll implement tail + parse loop in Swift. quick pseudo:
```swift
var tail = Data()
func onChunk(_ chunk: Data) {
  tail.append(chunk)
  while let (obj, consumed) = tryParseTopLevelJSON(from: tail) {
    handle(obj)
    tail.removeFirst(consumed)
  }
  if tail.count > 1_000_000 { // safety
    log("tail too big, resetting")
    tail.removeAll()
  }
}
```

josh: looks good. make sure tryParseTopLevelJSON distinguishes incomplete vs invalid. in Swift JSONSerialization throws for invalid only; you may need a streaming decoder or wrap with incremental parsing.

sam: i'll add a small test harness that simulates split points including multibyte boundaries and 1-byte-at-a-time delivery. can run in CI.

leo: i can add a small perf test too to ensure tail buffer doesn't regress memory under high QPS. we had a bug where tail kept growing when a bug caused tryParse to always return 0 consumed.

maria: thanks. action items: i'll open PR with reassembly util + unit tests for split emoji; sam adds CI harness; leo adds perf guard.

sre-bot: noted — tagging eng-oncall for visibility @eng-oncall.

maria: thanks all. ping me if you want to pair on the Swift parser.

josh: optional follow-up: should we make a small cross-sdk util in devex that each client can import? would reduce duplication.

anika: yup would be useful — a reference implementation in go/python/swift could live under devex/sdk-utils. low-pri but nice.

maria: will track as a follow-up issue. closing thread once PR lands. :thumbsup:
